title: Cranial Nerves VII–XII
summary: Face, hearing, swallowing, speech and tongue.

lessons.title: Facial Nerve

levels.kid:
Cranial nerve number 7 is the facial nerve. It is the nerve that lets you make faces!

When you smile, frown, wink, raise your eyebrows or puff your cheeks, nerve 7 is pulling the strings on your face muscles.

It does secret jobs too. It helps you taste sweet and salty things on the front of your tongue. It helps make tears and spit. It even turns down very loud sounds inside your ear.

Sometimes nerve 7 gets swollen and stops working for a while. Then one side of the face droops and can't smile or close the eye. Most of the time it gets better in a few weeks.
levels.hs:
**CN VII, the facial nerve**, controls the **muscles of facial expression**: smiling, frowning, closing the eyes and wrinkling the forehead. It also has smaller jobs:

- **Taste** from the front two-thirds of the tongue (through a branch called the **chorda tympani**)
- **Tears and saliva**: it stimulates the lacrimal gland and two salivary glands (submandibular and sublingual)
- **Stapedius**: a tiny ear muscle that dampens loud sounds

The nerve leaves the brainstem at the pons–medulla junction, travels with the hearing nerve into the temporal bone, winds through a narrow bony tunnel, and exits below the ear. It then passes through the parotid gland and fans out into five branches across the face.

Doctors use a key clue to tell where facial weakness comes from:

- **Upper motor neuron lesion** (like a stroke in the brain): only the **lower** face is weak. The forehead still wrinkles, because each side of the forehead gets signals from both sides of the brain.
- **Lower motor neuron lesion** (the nerve itself): the **whole side** of the face is weak, forehead included.

The most common cause of sudden one-sided facial weakness of the whole face is **Bell's palsy**. Most people recover, and steroids given early improve the chances. Because the eye may not close, protecting it from drying out is essential.
levels.college:
**Components.** Branchial motor (muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric); parasympathetic (lacrimal, nasal and palatine glands via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion; submandibular and sublingual glands via the chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion); taste (anterior two-thirds of the tongue, cell bodies in the **geniculate ganglion**, central fibers to the solitary nucleus), plus some ear sensation. The sensory and parasympathetic fibers travel as the **nervus intermedius**.

**Course.** Facial motor nucleus (caudal pons) → internal genu around the abducens nucleus → exit at the cerebellopontine angle → internal acoustic meatus → facial canal: **labyrinthine segment** (narrowest; geniculate ganglion; greater petrosal nerve branches off), **tympanic segment**, **mastoid segment** (nerve to stapedius, chorda tympani) → **stylomastoid foramen** → parotid → temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.

**UMN vs LMN.** The part of the facial nucleus supplying the upper face receives bilateral corticobulbar input; the lower face gets mainly contralateral input. A cortical or capsular lesion causes contralateral **lower-face** weakness with forehead sparing. A nuclear or nerve lesion causes ipsilateral weakness of the whole half-face.

**Localizing along the canal:**
- Proximal to the geniculate ganglion: dry eye, plus everything below
- Between geniculate and stapedius nerve: hyperacusis, taste loss, reduced saliva
- Between stapedius nerve and chorda tympani: taste loss, reduced saliva
- At the stylomastoid foramen or parotid: weakness only

**Causes of LMN palsy.** **Bell's palsy** (idiopathic, possibly herpes simplex reactivation; corticosteroids started within 72 hours improve recovery), **Ramsay Hunt syndrome** (varicella zoster: ear vesicles, pain, often hearing loss or vertigo), Lyme disease (often bilateral), Guillain–Barré, sarcoidosis, temporal bone fracture, parotid tumors, and CPA tumors.

**Sequelae.** Aberrant regeneration causes **synkinesis** (the eye closes when the mouth moves) and "crocodile tears" (tearing while eating). **Hemifacial spasm** is involuntary twitching, often from vascular compression at the root exit zone.
levels.phd:
**Two motor systems for one face.** Voluntary and emotional facial movements use partly separate pathways. Voluntary movements depend on primary motor and premotor cortex; spontaneous emotional expressions, such as a genuine smile, depend more on the cingulate motor areas, insula and subcortical circuits including the basal ganglia and thalamus. This creates a double dissociation: after a motor cortex or internal capsule stroke, a patient may be unable to smile on command but smile normally at a joke (**volitional facial paresis**), while lesions of the insula, thalamus or striatum can produce weakness only during emotional expression (**emotional facial paresis**). Primate tracing studies showing cingulate projections to the upper-face part of the facial nucleus offer one explanation for forehead sparing beyond the classic bilateral corticobulbar input.

**Bell's palsy pathogenesis.** The leading hypothesis is reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus in the geniculate ganglion, causing inflammation and swelling within the narrow labyrinthine segment of the canal, where the nerve almost fills the bony channel. Evidence includes viral DNA detected in some cases, but results are inconsistent, and antivirals add little or no clear benefit over steroids in trials. The narrow-segment entrapment model explains why steroids help and why some surgeons have argued for decompression in severe cases, a practice still debated.

**Electrophysiological prognosis.** Electroneuronography compares the compound muscle response on the affected side with the healthy side. If more than about 90 percent of fibers have degenerated in the first two weeks, the chance of poor recovery rises sharply. Wallerian degeneration takes several days to appear, so testing too early can mislead.

**Hemifacial spasm mechanisms.** Two models compete: ephaptic transmission between demyelinated axons at the root exit zone, and hyperexcitability of the facial motor nucleus driven by chronic irritation. The abnormal "lateral spread response," in which stimulating one branch activates muscles of another, typically disappears when the offending vessel is moved during surgery, and its disappearance has been studied as a predictor of cure.
levels.expert:
**Forehead first.** In any facial weakness, check the forehead. Sparing points to a central lesion and changes everything: a sudden central facial palsy with arm weakness or speech problems is a stroke alert. Beware partial peripheral palsies that seem to spare the forehead.

**Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion.** Red flags include slow progression over weeks, recurrence on the same side, involvement of only some branches, other cranial nerve deficits, a parotid mass, or no recovery by about three to four months; these demand imaging for a tumor such as a facial schwannoma or parotid malignancy. Eye care is not optional: lubrication, taping at night and sometimes eyelid weights prevent corneal ulcers.

**Trauma.** Temporal bone fractures that cross the otic capsule more often injure the facial nerve. Immediate complete paralysis after trauma (as opposed to delayed onset, which usually recovers) suggests the nerve may be cut or compressed; with severe degeneration on electrical testing, surgical exploration and decompression may be considered.

**Skull base surgery.** In vestibular schwannoma surgery, preserving facial function is often the main measure of success. EMG monitoring and direct stimulation track the nerve; the end-of-case stimulation threshold helps predict outcome. Surgeons sometimes leave a small amount of tumor on the nerve rather than risk paralysis, then watch it or treat with radiosurgery.

**Reanimation.** If the nerve is cut, primary repair or grafting gives the best results. If the facial muscles are still viable but the proximal nerve is unavailable, donor nerves such as the masseteric branch of V3 or part of the hypoglossal nerve can be connected to the facial nerve. For long-standing paralysis with wasted muscles, a free gracilis muscle transfer can restore a smile. Timing matters, since facial muscles deteriorate after roughly 1–2 years without nerve input.

**Hemifacial spasm.** Botulinum toxin injections are first-line; microvascular decompression, usually of AICA or PICA at the root exit zone, offers a potential cure with a risk of hearing loss.

keyPoints: CN VII: facial expression muscles, stapedius, taste (anterior 2/3 tongue), tears and saliva.
Course: pontomedullary junction → internal acoustic meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → parotid → 5 branches.
UMN lesion spares the forehead (bilateral input); LMN lesion weakens the whole half-face.
Bell's palsy: idiopathic LMN palsy; early steroids improve recovery; protect the eye.
Ramsay Hunt = VZV with ear vesicles; bilateral palsy suggests Lyme, GBS or sarcoidosis.
Aberrant regeneration causes synkinesis and crocodile tears.

examples.tr: Right LMN facial palsy, most likely Bell's palsy; start steroids early and protect the eye.

examples.src: A woman suddenly can't smile on the left, but her forehead wrinkles normally; her left arm is weak.
examples.tr: Central (UMN) facial weakness from a right hemisphere stroke: stroke alert.

examples.src: A patient with painful blisters in his ear canal develops facial palsy and hearing loss on the same side.

lessons.title: Vestibulocochlear Nerve

levels.kid:
Cranial nerve number 8 has two jobs, so it is like two nerves in one cable.

The first job is hearing. Deep inside your ear is a tiny snail-shaped tube with little hairs. When sound waves wiggle the hairs, nerve 8 sends the sound to your brain.

The second job is balance. Next to the snail are three loops filled with fluid. When you spin around, the fluid sloshes, and nerve 8 tells your brain which way you're moving.

That's why you feel dizzy after spinning in circles: the fluid keeps sloshing even after you stop!
levels.hs:
**CN VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve**, carries two senses from the inner ear in the temporal bone: **hearing** (cochlear part) and **balance** (vestibular part). It enters the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, next to the facial nerve, in a space called the **cerebellopontine angle**.

**Hearing.** Sound vibrates the eardrum and middle-ear bones, moving fluid inside the snail-shaped **cochlea**. Hair cells there turn the motion into nerve signals. Signals travel through brainstem relays to the temporal lobe. Because hearing pathways connect to both sides early, a stroke in the brain rarely causes deafness in one ear; one-sided hearing loss usually means a problem in the ear or the nerve.

Doctors use tuning-fork tests. Hearing loss can be **conductive** (sound can't get in, like with earwax or fluid) or **sensorineural** (the cochlea or nerve is damaged). Sudden sensorineural hearing loss in one ear is an emergency that needs urgent treatment.

**Balance.** Three **semicircular canals** sense head rotation, and two organs, the **utricle and saccule**, sense gravity and straight-line movement. The vestibular system keeps your eyes steady when your head moves. This is the **vestibulo-ocular reflex**.

Damage causes **vertigo**, a false sense of spinning. A common harmless cause is loose crystals in a canal (BPPV). A slow-growing tumor called a **vestibular schwannoma** can cause hearing loss and ringing in one ear.
levels.college:
**Cochlear pathway.** Inner hair cells in the organ of Corti → spiral ganglion neurons → cochlear nerve → **dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei** → bilateral **superior olivary complex** (medial superior olive: interaural time differences; lateral superior olive: interaural level differences) → **lateral lemniscus** → **inferior colliculus** → **MGN** → primary auditory cortex (**Heschl's gyrus**). Bilateral ascent means unilateral hearing loss localizes to the cochlea, nerve or cochlear nuclei.

**Bedside tests:**
- **Rinne**: air conduction normally louder than bone conduction; bone louder in conductive loss.
- **Weber**: sound lateralizes **toward** a conductive loss and **away from** a sensorineural loss.
- Formal audiometry confirms the type and severity.

**Vestibular system.** Semicircular canals detect angular acceleration; the utricle and saccule (otolith organs) detect linear acceleration and gravity. Primary afferents (cell bodies in the vestibular, or Scarpa's, ganglion) reach the **vestibular nuclei**, which project through the **MLF** to CN III, IV and VI (vestibulo-ocular reflex), to the spinal cord (vestibulospinal tracts), to the cerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) and to the thalamus.

**Vertigo, peripheral vs central:**
- **BPPV**: brief positional vertigo; diagnosed with the Dix–Hallpike maneuver and treated with repositioning (Epley).
- **Vestibular neuritis**: days of continuous vertigo without hearing loss.
- **Ménière disease**: episodic vertigo with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and ear fullness.
- **Central causes**: cerebellar or brainstem stroke, MS, vestibular migraine.

**HINTS exam** in acute continuous vertigo with nystagmus: a **normal head impulse test**, **direction-changing nystagmus** or a **skew deviation** each suggests a central cause. New hearing loss adds concern for AICA stroke ("HINTS plus"). In trained hands HINTS can be more sensitive than early MRI for posterior circulation stroke.

**Vestibular schwannoma.** A benign Schwann cell tumor of the vestibular nerve in the internal acoustic canal. It causes progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. Bilateral tumors define **NF2-related schwannomatosis**.
levels.phd:
**Mechanotransduction.** Hair cell stereocilia are linked at their tips by **tip links**. Deflection toward the tallest stereocilia tensions the links and opens mechanotransduction channels, with TMC1 and TMC2 now regarded as core pore-forming components. Potassium-rich endolymph and the endocochlear potential provide a large driving force, so transduction is fast and sensitive enough to detect motions near atomic dimensions.

**The cochlear amplifier.** Outer hair cells change length with voltage through the motor protein **prestin**, amplifying basilar membrane motion and sharpening frequency tuning. A byproduct is **otoacoustic emissions**, sounds produced by the ear itself, used to screen newborn hearing.

**Hidden hearing loss.** In mice, noise exposure that causes only temporary threshold shifts can permanently destroy synapses between inner hair cells and auditory nerve fibers (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009). Low spontaneous-rate fibers, important for hearing in noise, seem most vulnerable. Because the audiogram can stay normal, this "cochlear synaptopathy" may explain difficulty hearing in noisy places despite normal tests. Evidence in humans is suggestive but mixed.

**Gene therapy.** Mutations in **OTOF**, which encodes otoferlin (needed for synaptic release from inner hair cells), cause deafness with functioning hair cells. Early clinical trials of viral gene delivery into the cochlea, reported in 2024, described meaningful hearing gains in some children. Long-term durability and effects in other genetic forms remain to be established.

**VOR plasticity.** The vestibulo-ocular reflex must stay accurately calibrated as eyes, glasses and heads change. Its gain adapts through learning in the cerebellar **flocculus**, guided by retinal slip error signals carried by climbing fibers, with longer-term storage partly transferred to the vestibular nuclei. This is a classic model of cerebellar motor learning and underlies vestibular rehabilitation after unilateral loss, which relies heavily on central compensation.
levels.expert:
**The dizzy patient is a triage problem.** Most dizziness is benign, but a small fraction is posterior circulation stroke, and those patients are the ones most likely to be sent home wrongly. Sort by timing and triggers: brief, triggered by position (BPPV); spontaneous episodic (Ménière, vestibular migraine, TIA); continuous acute vestibular syndrome (neuritis or stroke). Use the HINTS exam only in continuous vertigo with nystagmus; a normal head impulse test in that setting is the dangerous result. Many posterior strokes are missed on early CT, and even MRI in the first day or two can be negative.

**Vestibular schwannoma management.** Options depend on size, growth, hearing and patient goals:
- **Observation** with serial MRI for small tumors, many of which do not grow
- **Stereotactic radiosurgery** for small and medium tumors, with high rates of growth control
- **Microsurgery** for large tumors compressing the brainstem, or by preference

Surgical approaches trade hearing for exposure. **Retrosigmoid** and **middle fossa** approaches can preserve hearing; **translabyrinthine** sacrifices hearing but gives wide exposure with minimal brain retraction and early identification of the facial nerve. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials and direct cochlear nerve recordings are used for hearing preservation attempts. Facial nerve outcome often weighs as heavily as tumor control.

**Hearing rehabilitation.** Cochlear implants bypass hair cells but need a working cochlear nerve. In NF2-related schwannomatosis, where both nerves may be lost, an **auditory brainstem implant** stimulates the cochlear nucleus directly, usually providing sound awareness and help with lip-reading rather than open-set speech understanding.

**Sudden sensorineural hearing loss** is an otologic emergency: early corticosteroids (oral or injected through the eardrum) and MRI to exclude a schwannoma. Asymmetric hearing loss on any audiogram should trigger an MRI of the internal acoustic canals.

**Superior canal dehiscence**, a thin or absent bone over the superior canal, causes sound- or pressure-induced vertigo and hearing one's own eye movements; it can be repaired through a middle fossa approach.

keyPoints: CN VIII = cochlear (hearing) + vestibular (balance); enters at the cerebellopontine angle with CN VII.
Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGN → Heschl's gyrus.
Central auditory pathways are bilateral, so unilateral hearing loss = ear, nerve or cochlear nucleus.
Weber lateralizes toward conductive loss and away from sensorineural loss; Rinne: bone > air in conductive loss.
Canals sense rotation; utricle/saccule sense gravity and linear motion; VOR keeps the eyes steady.
HINTS: normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew = central (stroke) until proven otherwise.

lessons.title: Glossopharyngeal & Vagus Nerves

levels.kid:
Cranial nerves 9 and 10 are teammates that live in your throat area.

Nerve 9 helps you taste with the back of your tongue and feel things in your throat. If something tickles the back of your throat, nerve 9 notices and you gag, which keeps you from choking.

Nerve 10 is called the vagus nerve. Vagus means "wanderer," because it wanders a long way down from your brain into your chest and tummy. It helps you swallow and talk, slows your heart down when you rest, and helps your tummy digest food.

Together, these two nerves help you eat, talk and stay safe from choking.
levels.hs:
**CN IX, the glossopharyngeal nerve**, and **CN X, the vagus nerve**, both leave the side of the medulla and exit the skull through the **jugular foramen**. They team up on swallowing and gagging.

**CN IX** ("tongue and throat"):
- Taste and general sensation from the back third of the tongue
- Sensation from the throat: the sensory side of the **gag reflex**
- Signals from the **carotid sinus** (blood pressure sensor) and **carotid body** (oxygen sensor)
- Saliva from the parotid gland

**CN X** ("wanderer") travels down the neck in the carotid sheath into the chest and abdomen:
- Muscles of the **palate, throat and voice box** (larynx): swallowing and speech; the motor side of the gag reflex
- **Parasympathetic** control: it slows the heart and drives digestion in much of the gut
- Sensation from organs, the larynx and part of the ear

Its **recurrent laryngeal** branch loops into the chest and back up to the voice box. On the left it hooks under the aorta. Because of this long path, a tumor in the chest or an injury during thyroid or neck surgery can cause a **hoarse voice**.

To test these nerves, doctors ask the patient to say "ahh." Normally the palate rises evenly. If one vagus nerve is weak, the uvula is pulled **toward the healthy side**.
levels.college:
**CN IX components.** Branchial motor to stylopharyngeus (nucleus ambiguus); parasympathetic to the parotid (inferior salivatory nucleus → tympanic and lesser petrosal nerves → **otic ganglion** → auriculotemporal nerve); taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, pharynx, tonsils and middle ear; visceral afferents from the **carotid sinus** (baroreceptors) and **carotid body** (chemoreceptors) via the carotid sinus nerve to the solitary nucleus.

**CN X components.** Branchial motor (nucleus ambiguus) to pharyngeal constrictors, soft palate (except tensor veli palatini, V3) and larynx; parasympathetic (**dorsal motor nucleus**) to the heart, lungs and gut as far as roughly the splenic flexure; visceral afferents to the solitary nucleus; sensation from larynx, pharynx and part of the ear canal (touching it can trigger a cough).

**Course.** Both exit the postolivary sulcus and leave through the **jugular foramen** with CN XI and the internal jugular vein. The vagus descends in the carotid sheath.

**Laryngeal branches:**
- **Superior laryngeal**: internal branch (sensation above the vocal folds), external branch (cricothyroid, pitch)
- **Recurrent laryngeal**: all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles and sensation below the folds; loops under the **right subclavian** artery and, on the left, under the **aortic arch** by the ligamentum arteriosum

**Exam.** Palate elevation and uvula (deviates **away** from the weak side), gag reflex (IX afferent, X efferent), voice quality, cough, and a water swallow screen. Gag loss alone is common in healthy people.

**Lesions:**
- Unilateral recurrent laryngeal palsy: hoarseness, weak cough; causes include thyroid and anterior neck surgery, lung apex or mediastinal tumors, and aortic arch enlargement (Ortner syndrome)
- **Jugular foramen (Vernet) syndrome**: IX, X, XI; adding XII suggests a lesion below the skull base (Collet–Sicard); causes include paragangliomas, schwannomas, metastases
- **Glossopharyngeal neuralgia**: shock-like throat or ear pain on swallowing, occasionally with syncope from vagal reflexes
levels.phd:
**The vagus is mostly sensory.** Roughly 80 percent of vagal fibers are afferent, carrying information from the heart, lungs, gut and immune organs to the solitary nucleus. Genetic labeling in mice has revealed distinct vagal sensory neuron types tuned to stomach stretch, intestinal nutrients, lung inflation and other signals, each linked to specific reflexes or behaviors. This molecular map is reshaping the idea of **interoception**, the brain's sense of the body's internal state, and the gut–brain axis.

**The inflammatory reflex.** Tracey and colleagues described a circuit in which vagal signaling reduces cytokine release from immune cells, partly through the spleen and the alpha-7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor on macrophages. The anatomy is debated, since the vagus does not appear to innervate the spleen directly and the pathway may run through the splenic sympathetic nerve. Small clinical studies of vagus nerve stimulation in rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease have shown encouraging results, and larger trials are under way.

**Vagus nerve stimulation in the brain.** Implanted VNS is approved for drug-resistant epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression, and VNS paired with rehabilitation is approved for arm recovery after stroke. Proposed mechanisms include activation of the locus coeruleus and basal forebrain through the solitary nucleus, releasing noradrenaline and acetylcholine that promote plasticity. Transcutaneous stimulation of the ear branch is being studied widely, but whether it reliably engages the same pathways is uncertain.

**Laterality.** The right vagus has stronger input to the sinoatrial node and the left to the atrioventricular node. Clinical VNS is placed on the left, partly to reduce the risk of bradycardia, although cardiac effects can still occur.

**Baroreflex physiology.** Carotid sinus afferents fire with each pressure pulse. Their input to the solitary nucleus inhibits sympathetic output and increases vagal tone. Electrical baroreflex activation therapy has been tested for resistant hypertension and heart failure, with mixed results.
levels.expert:
**Lower cranial nerves decide whether a patient can eat and breathe safely.** After surgery in the posterior fossa, skull base or neck, a new IX/X deficit means aspiration risk. Before oral intake, a formal swallow evaluation (bedside, then videofluoroscopy or endoscopic assessment) is routine. Bilateral deficits may need a feeding tube and sometimes a tracheostomy. Unilateral vocal fold paralysis can be improved with injection medialization or thyroplasty, often early, to restore cough and voice.

**Anterior cervical spine surgery.** Approaches to the cervical spine through the front of the neck retract the trachea and esophagus and can stretch the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness, usually temporary. Surgeons debate whether a left or right approach is safer; the longer, more predictable course of the left nerve is one argument for the left side, but evidence for a difference is weak. Reducing endotracheal cuff pressure after retractor placement is one strategy used to protect the nerve.

**Carotid endarterectomy.** The vagus lies in the carotid sheath, usually behind and between the carotid artery and the jugular vein. The hypoglossal and superior laryngeal nerves are also near the field. Careful dissection and avoiding clamping the vagus are standard.

**Jugular foramen tumors.** Paragangliomas (glomus jugulare) are highly vascular, often need preoperative embolization, and may secrete catecholamines. Because surgery can cause new lower cranial nerve palsies, many patients, especially older ones with preserved function, are treated with radiosurgery or observation.

**VNS implantation.** The lead is wrapped around the left vagus in the neck. During intraoperative testing, transient bradycardia or even asystole has been reported, so anesthesia monitors closely. Common side effects afterward are hoarseness and cough during stimulation.

**Clinical pearls.** Hoarseness with a normal throat exam needs laryngoscopy and imaging along the whole recurrent laryngeal course, from skull base to chest. Gag absence alone is not a reliable sign of aspiration risk.

lessons.title: Accessory & Hypoglossal Nerves

levels.kid:
Cranial nerve 11 and cranial nerve 12 are both about moving things.

Nerve 11 works two big muscles in your neck and shoulders. One helps you turn your head to look around. The other helps you shrug your shoulders, like when you say "I don't know!"

Nerve 12 works your tongue. Your tongue is a super flexible bundle of muscles. Nerve 12 lets you stick it out, lick an ice cream cone and move food around while you chew. It also helps you make sounds like "la la la."

If nerve 12 on one side gets hurt, the tongue leans to that side when you stick it out.
levels.hs:
**CN XI, the accessory nerve**, is unusual: its motor neurons are in the upper **spinal cord** (roughly C1 to C5). Its rootlets travel **up** through the foramen magnum into the skull, then turn around and exit through the **jugular foramen**. It supplies two muscles:

- **Sternocleidomastoid (SCM)**: turns the head to the **opposite** side and helps tilt it
- **Trapezius**: shrugs the shoulders and holds the shoulder blade in place

Doctors test shrugging and head turning against resistance. Damage causes a weak shrug, a drooping shoulder and difficulty raising the arm overhead. Because the nerve runs close to the surface in the side of the neck, it can be injured during lymph node surgery there.

**CN XII, the hypoglossal nerve** ("under the tongue"), controls almost all of the **tongue muscles**. Its nucleus is in the medulla, and it exits the skull through its own opening, the **hypoglossal canal**.

When you stick your tongue out, both sides push forward equally. If one hypoglossal nerve is damaged, that side is weak, and the tongue **points toward the damaged side**. Over time, the weak side may shrink (atrophy) and show small twitches (**fasciculations**). Tongue fasciculations are an important clue in **ALS**, a disease of motor neurons.

Both matter daily: the tongue for speech and swallowing, the trapezius for lifting.
levels.college:
**Accessory nerve.** Lower motor neurons sit in the **spinal accessory nucleus** in the upper cervical ventral horn (about C1–C5). Rootlets emerge laterally, ascend through the foramen magnum and exit with IX and X through the **jugular foramen**. The so-called cranial root, from the caudal nucleus ambiguus, joins the vagus and is now usually considered part of CN X. The nerve pierces the SCM and crosses the **posterior triangle** superficially to reach the trapezius.

**Testing:** head rotation against resistance (right SCM turns the head left), shrug and arm abduction above 90 degrees.

**Lesions:**
- Peripheral (posterior triangle surgery, lymph node biopsy, neck dissection, penetrating injury): trapezius weakness, shoulder droop, **lateral scapular winging**, pain; the SCM is often spared because its branch leaves first.
- Jugular foramen: SCM and trapezius both weak, with IX and X signs.
- Supranuclear: a hemispheric lesion usually weakens the **ipsilateral SCM** (difficulty turning the head toward the weak limbs) and contralateral trapezius, reflecting likely ipsilateral cortical control of SCM.

**Hypoglossal nerve.** The **hypoglossal nucleus** lies near the midline in the medulla (hypoglossal trigone). Fascicles run ventrally and exit in the **preolivary sulcus**, then leave through the **hypoglossal canal**. The nerve descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, hooks forward around the occipital artery, and runs above the hyoid to the tongue. It supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except **palatoglossus** (CN X). C1 fibers (ansa cervicalis, geniohyoid) hitchhike with it.

**Lesions:**
- **LMN**: tongue deviates **toward** the lesion, with atrophy and fasciculations (ALS, skull base tumors, carotid dissection, occipital condyle fractures, medial medullary stroke).
- **UMN**: tongue deviates **away from** the cortical lesion, without atrophy; often mild because of bilateral input.

Evaluate the tongue at rest in the mouth for fasciculations, since a protruded tongue often twitches normally.
levels.phd:
**What kind of nerve is CN XI?** The accessory nerve's neurons lie in the cervical spinal cord, yet their axons exit laterally like branchial motor nerves rather than through ventral roots. Developmental studies show these neurons share molecular features with hindbrain branchiomotor neurons, including dorsal axon exit guided by specific transcription factors and guidance receptors. This has fueled debate about whether SCM and trapezius are best viewed as branchial (pharyngeal arch-derived) or somatic muscles; lineage tracing in mice suggests they arise from mesoderm at the head–trunk boundary and share genetic programs with branchial muscles, so neither label fits perfectly.

**The tongue as a muscular hydrostat.** Like an octopus arm, the tongue has no bones; its intrinsic muscles (longitudinal, transverse, vertical) change shape while keeping volume constant, and extrinsic muscles move it as a whole. Hypoglossal motor neurons are organized into protrusor and retractor pools with a rough musculotopic map within the nucleus. This organization matters for therapies that target specific branches.

**Sleep and the genioglossus.** The genioglossus, the main tongue protruder, keeps the upper airway open. During sleep, especially REM, hypoglossal motor neuron excitability falls because of reduced serotonergic and noradrenergic drive and active inhibition, which can let the tongue fall back and close the airway in susceptible people. This is a central mechanism in **obstructive sleep apnea** and the basis of hypoglossal nerve stimulation.

**Motor neuron disease.** In bulbar-onset ALS, tongue atrophy and fasciculations can appear early. Ultrasound and EMG of the tongue can detect fasciculations and denervation, and quantitative tongue measures are being explored as disease markers. Notably, hypoglossal motor neurons degenerate in ALS while oculomotor neurons are largely spared, despite both being cranial motor neurons, a contrast used to search for protective molecular factors.

**Neuroplasticity after nerve transfer.** When the hypoglossal nerve is used to reanimate the face, patients initially move the face by pushing their tongue. Over months, some learn to smile without moving the tongue, a remarkable example of cortical remapping.
levels.expert:
**Protecting CN XI in the neck.** The spinal accessory nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in minor neck surgery, typically a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle, where it is superficial. The result is shoulder pain and droop, weakness lifting the arm overhead and scapular winging, often noticed weeks later. If no recovery is seen within a few months (or immediately if the nerve was known to be cut), exploration with repair or grafting gives the best results when done early. In cancer neck dissections, surgeons preserve the nerve whenever oncologically safe, since shoulder dysfunction strongly affects quality of life.

**XI as a donor nerve.** In brachial plexus injuries, the distal spinal accessory nerve is often transferred to the suprascapular nerve to restore shoulder abduction and external rotation. The nerve is divided beyond the upper trapezius branches to protect the shrug.

**Hypoglossal nerve in surgery.** During carotid endarterectomy, a high carotid bifurcation brings the hypoglossal nerve into the field; it must be identified and protected, since bilateral injury can threaten the airway. In skull base and craniovertebral junction surgery, occipital condyle drilling and screws can injure it within the hypoglossal canal.

**Hypoglossal nerve stimulation.** For selected patients with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea who cannot tolerate CPAP, an implanted stimulator activates the protrusor branches of CN XII during sleep, moving the tongue forward. Patient selection includes the pattern of airway collapse on sleep endoscopy.

**Reanimation.** The hypoglossal nerve can be partly split and joined to the facial nerve to restore facial tone; partial techniques reduce tongue weakness compared with full division. The masseteric nerve is now often preferred as a donor because it causes less donor deficit.

**Exam pearls.** A unilateral XII palsy with neck pain and Horner syndrome suggests carotid dissection. Tongue atrophy with fasciculations plus limb findings points to ALS, which warrants EMG.

keyPoints: CN XI motor neurons sit in the upper cervical cord; rootlets ascend through the foramen magnum and exit the jugular foramen.
XI supplies sternocleidomastoid (turns head to the opposite side) and trapezius (shrug, scapular stability).
Posterior triangle injury: weak shrug, shoulder droop, lateral scapular winging; SCM often spared.
CN XII exits the hypoglossal canal and supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus (X).
LMN XII lesion: tongue deviates toward the lesion with atrophy and fasciculations; UMN: away from the cortical lesion.
Tongue fasciculations are a key clue to ALS; XII palsy + Horner + neck pain suggests carotid dissection.

lessons.title: Bulbar vs Pseudobulbar Palsy

levels.kid:
The bottom of the brainstem used to be called the "bulb," because it looks a bit like a flower bulb. It controls talking, swallowing and the tongue.

Two kinds of problems can make talking and swallowing hard.

In the first kind, the bulb itself or its nerves get hurt. The muscles get weak and floppy, like a deflated balloon. The tongue can get thin and twitchy.

In the second kind, the bulb is fine, but the messages from the top of the brain can't reach it. Then the muscles get stiff instead of floppy. Sometimes people laugh or cry suddenly, even when they don't feel that way.

Doctors check the tongue and listen to the voice to tell which kind it is.
levels.hs:
The medulla was once called the **bulb**, so "bulbar" muscles are those controlled by the lower cranial nerves (mainly IX, X and XII): the **palate, throat, voice box and tongue**. They are needed for speaking and swallowing.

**Bulbar palsy** is a **lower motor neuron** problem: the nuclei in the medulla, the nerves themselves, or the nerve-muscle connection are damaged.
- Speech sounds **weak, breathy and nasal**
- Swallowing is hard; drinks may come out of the nose
- The tongue is **wasted and twitching** (fasciculations)
- The gag reflex is weak or absent

**Pseudobulbar palsy** is an **upper motor neuron** problem: damage to the pathways from the cortex to these nuclei on **both sides** of the brain.
- Speech is **slow, strained and harsh**
- Swallowing is hard
- The tongue is **stiff and small** but not wasted
- Reflexes like the jaw jerk are **brisk**
- Often **pseudobulbar affect**: sudden laughing or crying that doesn't match how the person feels

Why does pseudobulbar palsy need damage on both sides? Most bulbar nuclei receive input from both hemispheres, so one-sided damage is usually covered by the other side.

Causes of bulbar palsy include ALS, Guillain–Barré syndrome and myasthenia gravis. Pseudobulbar palsy is caused by repeated strokes, MS, brain injury or ALS. ALS can cause both at once.
levels.college:
**Definitions.** Bulbar palsy = LMN weakness of muscles supplied by the medulla (IX, X, XII, often with VII and V motor involvement): lesions of nuclei (nucleus ambiguus, hypoglossal), nerves, neuromuscular junction or muscle. Pseudobulbar palsy = bilateral **corticobulbar** (UMN) lesions above the brainstem nuclei.

**Comparison:**
- Dysarthria: bulbar = **flaccid** (hypernasal, breathy, imprecise); pseudobulbar = **spastic** (slow, strained-strangled, harsh)
- Tongue: bulbar = wasted, fasciculating, weak; pseudobulbar = small, spastic, slow alternating movements, no wasting
- Jaw jerk: bulbar = normal or absent; pseudobulbar = **brisk**
- Gag: bulbar = reduced; pseudobulbar = normal or brisk
- Emotion: pseudobulbar = **pseudobulbar affect** (involuntary laughter or crying)
- Limbs: bulbar = may have LMN signs; pseudobulbar = usually bilateral UMN signs

**Causes of bulbar palsy:**
- Motor neuron: ALS (progressive bulbar palsy), spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease), polio
- Nerve: Guillain–Barré (bulbar variants), diphtheria, skull base tumors, jugular foramen lesions
- Brainstem: lateral or medial medullary stroke, syringobulbia, Chiari malformation, brainstem tumors
- Neuromuscular junction and muscle: **myasthenia gravis** (fatigable), **botulism** (descending paralysis with dilated pupils), oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy

**Causes of pseudobulbar palsy:** bilateral strokes (multiple lacunes or bilateral hemispheric infarcts), MS, traumatic brain injury, ALS, progressive supranuclear palsy, and anterior opercular lesions (Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome, with loss of voluntary but not automatic face and mouth movement).

**Workup.** Look at the tongue at rest, test the jaw jerk, listen to the speech, check fatigability (sustained upgaze, counting aloud), and examine limbs for mixed UMN/LMN signs. MRI of the brain and craniovertebral junction, EMG with nerve conduction (including tongue and limb muscles), and antibody testing (acetylcholine receptor, MuSK) follow. Swallowing safety is assessed early because aspiration is the main danger.
levels.phd:
**Bilateral corticobulbar control.** Most motor cranial nuclei receive substantial input from both hemispheres, which is why unilateral cortical lesions often cause only mild or transient dysphagia and dysarthria. Swallowing research shows that the pharyngeal motor cortex is often larger on one side, differing between individuals; dysphagia after unilateral stroke is more likely when the dominant swallowing hemisphere is hit, and recovery correlates with increased representation in the undamaged hemisphere. Pharyngeal electrical stimulation and transcranial magnetic stimulation aim to drive this plasticity, with mixed trial results.

**Pseudobulbar affect.** The traditional explanation is release of brainstem emotional motor programs from cortical inhibition. Parvizi and colleagues proposed instead that lesions in cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathways disrupt the cerebellum's role in matching emotional expression to context. The NMDA antagonist and sigma-1 agonist combined with quinidine to slow its metabolism, is approved for the condition, supporting a role for glutamatergic and sigma-1 modulation, though the mechanism is not settled.

**ALS biology.** Bulbar-onset ALS accounts for roughly a quarter to a third of cases and tends to progress faster. Nearly all ALS shows **TDP-43** protein aggregates. The most common genetic cause is a repeat expansion in **C9orf72**, which also causes frontotemporal dementia, linking the two as a spectrum. Neurofilament light chain in blood and CSF is a promising marker of the rate of neuron loss. The antisense oligonucleotide **tofersen** received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for ALS caused by SOD1 mutations, based mainly on lowering neurofilament levels; it is a landmark for gene-targeted therapy, though it applies to a small minority of patients.

**Kennedy disease.** Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy results from a CAG repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. It mainly affects men, causing slowly progressive bulbar and limb weakness with fasciculations, plus signs of mild androgen insensitivity such as gynecomastia. It shows how a hormone receptor mutation can cause selective motor neuron degeneration.
levels.expert:
**Swallowing and breathing come first.** Whether the cause is bulbar or pseudobulbar, the dangers are aspiration, malnutrition and respiratory failure. Every patient gets an early speech and swallowing assessment with instrumental testing when needed. Diet texture changes and postural techniques help, but in progressive disease a feeding tube is discussed early.

**ALS timing.** Guidelines suggest placing a gastrostomy tube before breathing becomes too weak, since the procedure carries more risk once vital capacity falls. Noninvasive ventilation improves survival and quality of life in patients with respiratory weakness, though bulbar patients may tolerate masks less well. Advance care planning, including decisions about tracheostomy and invasive ventilation, should happen while the patient can communicate easily; voice banking and eye-gaze devices preserve communication later.

**Do not miss the treatable mimics.**
- **Myasthenia gravis** can present with fatigable dysarthria and dysphagia, sometimes without obvious eye signs. Myasthenic crisis needs ICU monitoring of breathing and treatment with plasma exchange or immunoglobulin.
- **Botulism**: descending paralysis with dilated pupils and dry mouth; antitoxin given early.
- **Guillain–Barré variants** with bulbar weakness can progress to respiratory failure quickly.
- **Structural lesions**: a Chiari malformation, basilar invagination or a foramen magnum tumor can compress the lower brainstem and cause slowly progressive bulbar signs. Decompression can halt progression, so MRI of the craniovertebral junction is part of every unexplained bulbar workup.

**Neurosurgical patients.** After posterior fossa surgery, new bulbar weakness may not show until the patient tries to drink. Early extubation can fail from airway incompetence, so teams assess cough and secretion handling before extubation and keep the patient nil by mouth until swallow testing is done.

**Pseudobulbar affect** is often mistaken for depression. Ask directly; it is treatable and its recognition relieves patients and families. Pseudobulbar palsy after bilateral strokes often coexists with cognitive impairment, which affects swallowing safety and rehabilitation plans.

keyPoints: Bulbar palsy = LMN weakness of IX, X, XII muscles: flaccid nasal speech, wasted fasciculating tongue, weak gag.
Pseudobulbar palsy = bilateral corticobulbar (UMN) lesions: spastic speech, stiff small tongue, brisk jaw jerk.
Pseudobulbar affect: involuntary laughing or crying that doesn't match mood.
Bulbar causes: ALS, GBS, myasthenia, botulism, medullary stroke, syringobulbia, skull base lesions.
Pseudobulbar causes: bilateral strokes, MS, TBI, ALS, PSP; ALS can cause both.
First priorities: swallow safety, aspiration risk, breathing; MRI of the craniovertebral junction in unexplained cases.
